Based on the search results, here's what I found about Rosa damascena flower essential oil composition analyzed by GC-MS in Turkey:

## Cultivation in Turkey

Turkish Rose Oil is obtained from Rosa damascena roses, which are cultivated largely in Isparta, Burdur, Afyon and Denizli in Turkey. Turkey is a leading producer of R. damascena.

## Chemical Composition

GC-MS chromatograph profiles reveal significant presence of β-citronellol (30.24–31.15%), trans-geraniol (20.62–21.24%), n-heneicosane (8.79–9.05%), n-nonadecane (8.51–8.77%), nonadecene (4.42–4.55%) and phenylethyl alcohol (4.04%).

In another study, the dominant and main components of the essential oil were oleic acid (48.08%), palmitic acid (15.44%), stearic acid (10.17%), citronellol (7.37%) and nonadecane (3.70%).

## Analysis Methods

Studies have determined the composition of Rosa damascena essential oil from Turkey via GC-MS. Essential oil extraction is typically performed by hydrodistillation using a Clevenger apparatus.

## What is ISO 9842?

ISO 9842:2003 specifies characteristics of the oil of rose (Rosa x damascena Miller) in order to facilitate assessment of its quality. The standard specifies certain characteristics of the oil of rose (Rosa x damascena Miller) cultivated in Turkey, Morocco and Bulgaria, of the Rosaceae family, in order to facilitate assessment of its quality.

## About Rosa x damascena

Rosa Damascena is the most widely used rose variety in perfumery. Classified in the rose family, Rosa Damascena rose essential oil is one of the best-known perfumery ingredients, as it is prized for the diffusion, sensual quality, and sweetness that it gives to a composition. Besides perfume, this high quality rose oil is also used in cosmetics, medicine, and food markets.

## Geographic Origins and History

It originated from Iran and essential oil extracting from its flowers has been started since 7th century A.D. Nowadays, Bulgaria and Turkey are the main producers of R. damascena essential oil in the world, and the Bulgarian R. damascena oil is the known best ones.

## Testing Methods

The standard details that analysis of the essential oil should be carried out by gas chromatography.

Note: There is also a newer version—ISO 9842:2024 specifies quality characteristics and test methods for rose essential oil produced from Rosa x damascena cultivated in Turkey, Morocco and Bulgaria.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Turkish rose oil from Isparta, its citronellol/geraniol ratio, and comparison with Bulgarian rose oil:

## Turkish Rose Oil Origin and Production

Turkish rose is derived from Rosa x damascena cultivated primarily in the Isparta region, which is the finest of the Turkish rose oils and even has a special designation much in the same way that Champagne has in France.

## Citronellol and Geraniol Ratios

In Turkish rose oil, citronellol ranges from 24.47–42.97%, with geraniol at 2.11–18.04%. More specifically, Turkish rose has high citronellol content (up to 37%), and Turkish rose contains β-Citronellol at 25–37% and trans-Geraniol at 20–32%.

Regarding the citronellol/geraniol ratio specifically, in Turkish factory oils the citronellol/geraniol ratio is 2.30 to 4.84%, while village oils give a ratio of 0.83 to 1.92%.

## Comparison with Bulgarian Rose Oil

In Bulgarian rose oil the citronellol/geraniol ratio is around 1%, which is notably lower than Turkish oils. 

The chemical composition of Turkish Rose Otto is distinguishable from that of Bulgarian Rose Otto due to higher percentages of the two main components – citronellol and geraniol – resulting in a bit more sweetness and strength in the aroma. Additionally, Bulgarian oil is sweeter and more intense, while Turkish oils are fruitier, fresher and spicier.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about rose oil use levels, methyl eugenol, and IFRA regulations in perfumery:

## Rose Oil and Methyl Eugenol Content

Rose contains eugenol and methyl eugenol, both regulated under IFRA. Rose oil contains a small amount of methyl eugenol, and factors such as aquaculture practices, harvest and post-harvest processes and distillation practices affect the methyl eugenol content.

## IFRA Limits for Methyl Eugenol in Perfumery

Methyl eugenol as a fragrance is currently used at a rate of 0.3-0.8% in perfumes, 0.01-0.05% in creams and lotions, and 0.02-0.2% in soaps and detergents. More specifically for fine fragrance products, under the IFRA label of Methyl Eugenol, Fine fragrance is 0.01% and Eau de toilette is 0.004%.

## Eugenol Limits

For eugenol generally (distinct from methyl eugenol), for many leave-on products, the limit for eugenol is about 0.64% in finished formulations.

## Implications for Natural Rose Oil

Only the tiniest amounts of natural rose oil, basil oil, nutmeg and many others can be used unless they have been rectified to get rid of the methyl eugenol.
